title: Thérèse of Lisieux (1873–1897)
hook: she died at 24 in an obscure convent and became one of the most loved saints

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernadette at Lourdes, who dug where the spring appeared. Your line was she was only asked to tell. Did you say one true thing and let it go? Day ninety-three.

A girl of fourteen is in Rome with her father and a group of pilgrims, waiting in line to meet the Pope. They've all been told firmly: do not speak to the Holy Father. When her turn comes, she kneels, grabs his knees, and asks him anyway. She wants to enter a convent now, at fifteen, not years later. He tells her, gently, that she will enter if God wills it. She has to be carried away by the guards. A year later she's inside the Carmelite convent in the small French town of Lisieux. She'll never leave it. She'll die there at twenty-four, and almost nobody outside will have heard of her. Today, Thérèse.
screen: `A GIRL KNEELS BEFORE THE POPE.` → `A CONVENT AT FIFTEEN.` → `DEAD AT TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Thérèse Martin grew up the youngest of five sisters in a devout family. Her mother died when she was four, and she was a sensitive, tearful child. In the convent she read about the great saints, the martyrs and mystics, and felt tiny beside them. They were mountains. She was a grain of sand. So she went looking for a shortcut. She wrote that in her time, the rich had lifts to save them climbing stairs, and she wanted a lift to God, because she was too small to climb the rough stairway of perfection. She found it in a line of scripture. In the Douay-Rheims: "Whosoever is a little one, let him come to me." The lift, she decided, was the arms of Jesus. She didn't have to become big. She had to stay little and let herself be carried. That's the little way. In practice it looked ordinary. She smiled at a sister who grated on her nerves, so sweetly that the sister thought she was her favorite. When another nun splashed her with dirty water in the laundry, she took it without complaint. Small things, done with great love. In her last eighteen months, dying of tuberculosis, she also went through a deep darkness, when heaven felt closed to her, and she kept going anyway. Her notebooks became a book, Story of a Soul, published a year after she died. It spread around the world. She was canonized in 1925, and in 1997 she was named a Doctor of the Church, one of only a handful of women.
screen: `TOO SMALL FOR THE GREAT SAINTS.` · `A LIFT INSTEAD OF STAIRS.` · `SMALL THINGS, GREAT LOVE.` · `DARKNESS, AND SHE KEPT GOING.` · then, large: `WHOSOEVER IS A LITTLE ONE, LET HIM COME TO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one small thing to do with great love. Settle, and breathe. Look ahead at your day. Find the smallest, most forgettable task in it: washing a cup, answering a message, holding a door, listening to someone repeat a story. Choose one. Now picture doing it slowly and warmly, as if it mattered, because Thérèse would say it does. If you pray, you can offer it to God before you do it. The bell holds the time.
Thérèse of Lisieux. The Little Flower, who found a way to holiness for people who feel too small for it. Today's word.
Your line: the little way. Today, do the small thing you picked, with more love than it seems to need, and tell no one. Day ninety-three.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of St. Thérèse on October 1, read her autobiography Story of a Soul, and many ask her prayers in novenas; she is a patron of the missions, though she never left her convent.
